## What height adds to the regeneration story {#rd03-review}

Does retained overstory leave redwood with a developing cohort of tall sprouts,
even where regeneration basal area is strongly reduced? Height helps distinguish
the size attained by leading sprouts from the amount of regeneration occupying
an area. We'll review the thesis evidence before choosing a publication model
and the smallest useful set of displays. The publication's regeneration-first
direction makes redwood development the main question, with tanoak providing
ecological context; this task does not repeat RD02's basal-area result.

**Phase One is complete for the available records; field-history questions remain
for human review.** The [input audit and handoff](#rd03-phase-one) extend the
initial thesis review below. No publication models have been fitted and no new
model estimates, significance claims, or displays are accepted.

### Evidence reviewed and numerical limits

The review uses the thesis [Methods](../thesis/methods.html#sprout-heights),
[Results](../thesis/results.html#sprout-heights), and
[Discussion](../thesis/discussion.html#sprout-height), their QMD sources,
`analysis/analysis/sprouts_import_data.qmd`, and
`analysis/analysis/sprout_modeling.qmd`. On 6 November 2026 we also inspected
`analysis/sprout_modeling.rda` and `analysis/wrangled_sprouts.rda` read-only in
thesis R 4.3.2 with its existing library (glmmTMB 1.1.11). We checked saved calls,
model frames, coefficients, variance components, convergence flags, and
zero-random-effect predictions. Neither the thesis environment nor its saved
objects was changed. Its startup reported an out-of-sync project, locale warnings,
and a glmmTMB build under R 4.3.3; this inspection is not an environment validation.

The saved analysis contains 692 clumps: 334 redwood and 358 tanoak, across four
sites and 16 treatment-unit macro plots. There are 2,076 height observations and
1,384 increments, with no missing outcomes in these saved frames. Treatment
cell sizes range from 72 to 91 clumps for redwood and 78 to 95 for tanoak.
The imported increments exactly equal $(H_5-H_1)/4$ and $(H_{10}-H_5)/5$.
Those checks establish the content of the saved analysis, not the completeness
of the original field cohort or the reason clump counts differ.

At the initial review, committed publication exports covered fuels and
regeneration basal area, not sprout heights. An intentional sprout export in the thesis environment,
with identifiers, factor levels, missingness, selection information where
available, and historical prediction references, is a prerequisite for publication
fitting. We must also reconcile those exports with the original workbook and
field history before assuming that the complete saved frames imply no attrition.
The existing exporter and manifest should be extended when we implement the
analysis. Phase One below implements that boundary and documents what field
history remains unavailable.

## What the thesis models actually assume {#rd03-thesis-models}

The measured response is the **height of the tallest sprout within a selected
clump at each visit**. The leading stem can change between visits. Consequently,
the increment is change in clump maximum height, annualized over an interval,
rather than necessarily the elongation of one continuously tracked stem. The
saved variable named `tree` identifies the repeated clump record for this purpose.
It is not evidence that the same individual sprout remained tallest.

Clumps were selected to be well distributed within macro plots. Redwood sampling
also balanced clumps with and without residual standing trees. That is not a
documented equal-probability sample of all clumps or stems. An unweighted model
describes this selected clump cohort; generalizing to an area-wide clump mean
requires a defensible sampling assumption or known inclusion weights. It cannot
be interpreted as mean height of all regeneration, mean height of retained PCT
trees, survival, recruitment, or an area-based productivity measure.

### Interval height increment

The saved `minc_sel` is the source's `minc15`, with Gaussian response and identity
link. Writing `period` for the factor stored as `year` (5 = years 1–5;
10 = years 5–10), its conditional mean formula is:

`ht_inc ~ treat * spp + period * spp + (1 | clump) + (0 + spp | macro)`.

The source uses globally unique `tree` and `plot` IDs for `clump` and `macro`.
Residual dispersion is `~ spp * period * treat`, allowing 16 species–treatment–
period residual scales. The macro effect is a two-species unstructured covariance
matrix: separate species variances and one correlation, not a separate common
macro intercept plus an additional species effect. The clump intercept variance
is common to both species. There is no separate site term in this saved model.
The [glmmTMB covariance documentation](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/articles/covstruct.html)
explains the distinction between unstructured and diagonal species effects.

This specification allows species-specific treatment differences and
species-specific changes between periods. It **constrains the period change to
be identical across all treatments within a species**: neither treatment × period
nor the three-way mean interaction is present. A lack of those terms does not
establish equal temporal responses. Conditional residuals are independent after
the clump and macro effects; the clump intercept induces nonnegative covariance
between its two increments. Random effects are Gaussian, independent across
grouping levels, and independent of predictors. Residual heterogeneity does not
replace either clustering or a suitable within-clump covariance.

The saved fit reports convergence code 0 and a positive-definite Hessian. Clump
SD is 0.115 m yr^-1^; macro SDs are 0.141 for redwood and 0.059 for tanoak, with
correlation 0.254. These estimates support inspecting unequal species variation,
without establishing that this covariance structure is adequate or precisely
estimated from 16 macro plots.

### Height at year 10

The saved `ht10_sel` is `mht1011`, a Gaussian response with a log link:

`ht ~ treat * spp + (0 + spp | macro) + (1 | site)`;
residual dispersion is `~ spp * treat` (eight residual scales).

The response itself is not log-transformed. Residual variation is additive on
the metre scale, while the conditional mean is positive and multiplicative in
the predictors. A Gaussian distribution can still generate negative heights:
a log link restricts its mean, not its support. The model assumes a shared
site intercept on the log-mean scale and correlated species-specific macro
intercepts. No clump intercept is needed for one response per clump.

This fit also reports convergence code 0 and a positive-definite Hessian. Macro
SDs on the log-mean scale are 0.195 for redwood and 0.159 for tanoak, with
correlation 0.475. Site SD is approximately 0.000021, effectively at the boundary.
This is weak information about a site variance, not proof that blocking is
scientifically irrelevant. Four sites remain four treatment replicates per
treatment; the hundreds of clumps are subsamples.

## Validity and precision of the thesis interpretation {#rd03-interpretation}

### Patterns supported by the saved means

The following historical values were reproduced from the saved coefficients
and response predictions with random effects set to zero. They are not new
publication estimates. Increment means give the two intervals equal weight.

| Species | Increment GS | Increment LD | Increment HA | Increment HD | Year-10 height GS | Year-10 height HD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Redwood | 0.957 | 0.800 | 0.633 | 0.556 | 10.384 | 5.810 |
| Tanoak | 0.474 | 0.379 | 0.306 | 0.299 | 5.127 | 3.117 |

Increment units are m yr^-1^; height units are m. The extra digits make this
audit identifiable, not biologically precise. The year-10 means match the
rendered thesis's 10.38–5.81 m and 5.13–3.12 m ranges, rather than the older
10.29–6.16 m and 5.12–3.04 m values left in the modeling notebook.

The broad descriptive pattern is coherent: leading redwood sprouts were taller
and had larger increments than tanoak; GS means were largest; HA and HD were
lower, particularly for redwood. These observations add a size dimension to
RD02's area-based regeneration response. They do not establish every adjacent
treatment difference or a continuous response to measured light.

### Corrections needed before publication

1. **The model and prose disagree about interactions.** The thesis year-10
   Results say the model lacks species × treatment and therefore gives parallel
   treatment comparisons. The saved fit contains that interaction, as do the
   Methods' final specification. The increment notebook also says an interaction
   is absent after assigning a model that contains it. Distinguish an AIC-preferred
   reduced candidate from the retained research-question model. With a log link,
   omitting the interaction would impose common treatment *ratios*, not common
   metre differences. Nonsignificant interaction tests do not establish equivalence.

2. **The species response claim needs its own contrast.** In the retained
   increment model, treatment coefficients alone refer to the reference species,
   tanoak. Redwood treatment differences combine those coefficients with the
   interaction. A range of coefficient p values is not an omnibus treatment test.
   The saved redwood-versus-tanoak difference in the HD–GS increment response is
   about -0.227 m yr^-1^, with an individual asymptotic Wald p value of 0.029.
   This does not supply a multiplicity-adjusted family test, but it shows why
   the blanket statement that the interaction was nonsignificant is imprecise.
   Publication claims need explicitly defined contrasts and uncertainty.

3. **Period means mix historical versions and weighting conventions.** The
   text's 0.80 to 0.67 m yr^-1^ for redwood and 0.39 to 0.34 for tanoak agrees
   approximately with equally weighted treatment predictions (0.803 to 0.670;
   0.385 to 0.344). The thesis temporal prediction call uses `newdata = NULL`,
   averaging observed rows; that gives 0.804 to 0.672 and 0.384 to 0.342 in the
   saved fit. We should use one declared weighting rule and regenerate prose
   from its results. The period decreases are 0.132 and 0.041 m yr^-1^ in every
   treatment by model construction, not eight independently demonstrated changes.

4. **Equal-period averaging is not the nine-year annual rate.** The two intervals
   last four and five years. An equal-period mean is $(I_1+I_2)/2$; the annualized
   years 1–10 change is $(4I_1+5I_2)/9$. Neither includes years 0–1. Label these
   quantities explicitly; prefer separate intervals if temporal development is
   the scientific point.

5. **Response-scale prediction is not random-effect integration.** The thesis
   helper explicitly uses `re.form = NA`, setting random effects to zero, as
   described in the [prediction documentation](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/reference/predict.glmmTMB.html).
   For identity-link increments, zero-mean random-effect integration leaves the
   mean unchanged. For log-link year-10 height it gives
   $M_{st}=\exp\{x_{st}^{\mathsf T}\beta+(\tau^2_{\mathrm{site}}+
   \tau^2_{\mathrm{macro},s})/2\}$ under this model. This is integration over
   log-mean random effects; there is no lognormal *residual* correction for a
   Gaussian response with a log link. The current factors are about 1.019 for
   redwood and 1.013 for tanoak. The distinction is small here but must remain
   explicit, especially if we change the hierarchy or family. As in RD02,
   treatment-constant integration factors preserve within-species ratios.

6. **Asymptotic intervals have limited replication behind them.** The thesis
   prediction-to-emmeans helper uses `df = Inf` and reconstructs mean covariance
   from mean and pairwise-difference SEs. The resulting comparison arrows are
   not ordinary confidence bars or an independent validation of contrasts.
   Reproduce their covariance, contrast scale, and adjustment before retaining
   any historical pairwise claim. The printed `p = 0` is rounding, never an exact
   zero probability. New displays should show intervals for means and report
   selected contrasts separately. Model selection, sampling selection, measurement
   error, and covariance-structure uncertainty are not included in those Wald
   intervals. Convergence flags alone do not verify residual fit or interval coverage.

### What the biological interpretation can support

Tallest-clump height is relevant to the potential size of a future retained
sprout. It does not identify the stems actually retained after PCT or demonstrate
their subsequent performance. Height and basal area may respond differently
because one describes selected clump maxima and the other integrates stem sizes
and occurrence per area. That difference is informative rather than contradictory.

Treatments combine overstory amount and spatial arrangement. HA versus HD is the
direct arrangement comparison at similar target retention; a small, uncertain
difference does not establish that aggregation has no effect. The treatment
gradient is consistent with light limitation, but height models alone do not
isolate light from other treatment-associated conditions or establish a species'
physiological shade tolerance. An SDI or light model would ask a different question.

The thesis suggestion that roughly 32–38 m^2^ ha^-1^ is an upper retention bound
for sustaining redwood growth beyond ten years exceeds what four categorical
treatments and a ten-year record establish. We can say that leading redwood
sprouts continued gaining height under the studied high-retention treatments,
at lower estimated rates than GS. We cannot estimate a continuous threshold,
long-term sustainability, stand yield, or an optimal cutting cycle from these fits.

## Proposed revisions and sensitivity tests {#rd03-model-plan}

Our working target is **arithmetic mean tallest-clump height, or its interval
change, for the sampled clump cohort under each treatment**. We should standardize
comparisons across equally weighted treatments and sites and state whether means
average the four observed sites or integrate an exchangeable site population.
The latter matches RD02's presentation, but adds a generalization assumption that
four sites estimate poorly. Neither target automatically represents all clumps
per hectare. If field information supports redwood sampling-stratum weights,
report that explicitly rather than silently redefining the population.

We'll keep year-10 height as the primary size endpoint and interval increment
as the complementary temporal endpoint. Start with the thesis response families
as reference fits, retain species-specific treatment means, and test the following
limited alternatives. These are proposed candidates, not an invitation to choose
whichever produces the strongest treatment significance.

| Proposed change or test | Assumption retained, relaxed, or introduced | Evidence needed for a decision |
|---|---|---|
| Represent site blocking in both endpoints; compare site fixed effects with site random intercepts, retaining macro clustering | Replaces the increment model's independence of different treatment units at the same site. Fixed sites condition inference on these four blocks; random sites assume exchangeability and a Gaussian site distribution. | Treatment estimates and intervals under both specifications, variance boundaries, and four leave-one-site-out fits. Do not delete design clustering solely for AIC or a near-zero estimate. |
| Compare the joint unstructured species macro effects with diagonal effects and separate species fits, allowing species-specific clump variance for increments | Diagonal effects remove cross-species macro covariance; separate fits also remove shared variance constraints. The thesis shares clump variance across species. Separate species-specific site variances relax the common site variance but are weakly identified from four sites. | Same response rows and family for the covariance comparison; inspect variance estimates, correlations, optimizer agreement, and treatment uncertainty. Separate fits can describe species means but do not supply covariance for a species-difference test. |
| Retain treatment × species; compare increment means with `treat * spp * period` | Relaxes the imposed common period change across treatments. The full mean model permits treatment-specific slowing or acceleration within each species. | Period-change contrasts and their species/treatment differences, with intervals. Absence of a detected interaction is not temporal equivalence. A reduced model needs a scientific interpretation as well as fit support. |
| Compare saturated dispersion with `spp * period` and additive treatment dispersion for increments; `spp + treat` versus `spp * treat` for year 10 | Reduced dispersion pools residual scales across some cells. It does not pool treatment means or solve clustering. Separate-species fits permit their own residual scales. | Residual spread and tails by species, treatment, period, and macro plot; fit stability and changes in interval widths. Retain supported heterogeneity rather than simplifying to improve significance. |
| Test within-clump covariance of the two increments; compare the shared intercept with a directly estimated two-period covariance | The thesis allows only nonnegative residual association through a common clump intercept. An unstructured two-period covariance permits either sign and different variances, but needs an identifiable parameterization. | Estimate covariance after macro/site effects. Do not add a full two-period covariance on top of freely varying period residual variances and a clump intercept: these components cannot all be identified from two outcomes per clump. |
| Compare year-10 Gaussian identity/log links and positive Gamma(log); use a lognormal alternative only if residual evidence warrants it | Identity link models additive metre effects; log links model proportional conditional effects. Gamma imposes positive support and variance proportional to squared mean within a dispersion group. Lognormal assumes Gaussian log-height residuals and needs residual as well as random-effect integration for arithmetic means. | Observed/predicted distributions and lower-tail/negative-height simulation frequency, residual scale, convergence, and estimates on the same arithmetic-mean target. Do not use Gamma for increments if valid zero or negative increments exist in the audited input. |
| Fit heights at years 1, 5, and 10 jointly as a targeted sensitivity, with categorical age and identifiable within-clump covariance | Avoids treating two differences sharing year 5 as conditionally independent. Categorical age avoids assuming linear growth or extrapolating a curve from three visits. It introduces a model for the three-level covariance and all-age means. | Derive $(M_5-M_1)/4$, $(M_{10}-M_5)/5$, and year-10 means from one fit, retaining covariance. Compare these estimands with the two-endpoint analysis; use the joint model as primary only if its assumptions and stability are preferable. |
| Compare zero-effect, integrated, and observed-site standardized predictions; equal-period and duration-weighted summaries | Changes the prediction target or averaging weights, not necessarily the fitted model. Integration assumes the specified random-effect distribution represents the target population. | Reconcile implementation by direct prediction, analytic integration where available, and numerical checks. Propagate variance-parameter uncertainty for integrated means. Never label a change of estimand as a biological change. |

### Why the shared year-5 measurement matters

If measured heights have independent errors $e_1,e_5,e_{10}$, then the two
increment errors are $(e_5-e_1)/4$ and $(e_{10}-e_5)/5$. Their covariance is
$-\operatorname{Var}(e_5)/20$. A persistent clump growth tendency can instead
produce positive association. The thesis clump intercept represents the latter
but cannot by itself represent the former. This derivation does not prove that
the fitted covariance is wrong; it identifies a scientifically motivated
sensitivity with a possible consequence for uncertainty in growth-rate change.
With no replicate height measurements, measurement-error variance cannot be
separately learned without additional assumptions or external precision data.
Two intervals also cannot establish a general serial-correlation process.

### Selection and uncertainty sequence

First audit identity, measurement definitions, interval lengths, original missing
records, and any mortality or leader replacement notes. Resolve the redwood
residual-tree sampling stratum: its indicator is described in the import source
but omitted from the selected columns. If recoverable, use it for a targeted
sampling/composition sensitivity, recognizing that residual-tree status is
treatment-related and adjusting for it changes the question. Likewise, conditioning
on year-1 height estimates later development at a common *post-treatment* size;
it is not a correction for a pretreatment covariate and should not replace the
unadjusted treatment comparison. Do not treat absent/dead clumps as zero heights
without field justification, or invent missing-data weights from these complete
saved frames.

Next fit the reference and design/covariance alternatives on identical audited
rows. Use maximum likelihood when comparing fixed-effect structures. Compare
AIC within the same endpoint and likelihood basis; AIC across height and increment
responses is meaningless. A model for log(height) needs the response-transformation
Jacobian before comparing its likelihood with original-height models. Keep
scientific mean terms needed for planned contrasts even when their individual
coefficients are weak. Avoid stepwise selection over every interaction.

Require numerical convergence, a usable Hessian, and agreement under a second
optimizer for plausible finalists. Inspect boundary variances, residual and
simulation diagnostics by species/treatment/period, within-clump association,
macro-level residual patterns, and influential sites. Four leave-one-site-out
analyses diagnose sensitivity; they do not turn three-site fits into precise
estimates or justify dropping an inconvenient site. A small AIC difference or
nonsignificant diagnostic is weak evidence, as RD02 demonstrated.

Compare finalist mean estimates and intervals for GS versus HD (retention
contrast), HA versus HD (arrangement contrast), and the second-minus-first
interval change. Add species differences in those responses only with a joint
covariance model or a paired resampling method that preserves sites, macro plots,
and both species. Predeclare contrast families and a multiplicity approach
(for example Holm adjustment for a small confirmatory family); keep other
contrasts exploratory. GS–HD compares complete treatments, not an isolated
continuous basal-area effect. Use metre differences for size and m yr^-1^
differences for increment; report ratios as an additional interpretation only
when useful. Avoid claiming equal responses without a biologically justified
equivalence margin.

For the preferred specification, assess the sensitivity of Wald uncertainty with
a refitted parametric bootstrap that preserves the hierarchy, heterogeneity,
and repeated measurements, including variance-parameter uncertainty in integrated
means. Predeclare a seed and simulation count, report failed/boundary refits,
and examine stability of interval endpoints. This assesses inference under the
fitted model, not robustness to unmodeled sampling bias. Resampling just four
sites nonparametrically is a weak sole basis for coverage. A within-site treatment
randomization sensitivity is possible only after confirming the assignment
scheme in the experimental record; it tests a different, design-based null.
Intervals conditional on a selected model still omit model-selection uncertainty.

RD02 motivates design-aware clustering, explicit estimands, species-specific
variance checks, optimizer checks, and caution with four-site asymptotics. Its
hurdle-Gamma occurrence process does **not** transfer automatically: these
height records are selected clumps, not vegetation plots with recorded absence.
We should select the simplest scientifically adequate height model and report
material sensitivity, even if the treatment ordering remains unchanged.

## Proposed publication displays {#rd03-display-proposals}

### 1. Main figure: attained height and temporal change

Use one four-panel figure, with redwood and tanoak as columns. The top row shows
year-10 mean tallest-clump height by treatment (GS, LD, HA, HD), in metres, with
95% intervals. The bottom row shows the estimated change in annualized increment,
years 5–10 minus years 1–5, by treatment, with 95% intervals and a zero reference
line. Use a common height scale across species for direct size comparison and
a common increment-change scale across species in the bottom row. Keep the
species colors/shapes used in RD02 and state that the sampling units differ.

This joins attained size with the genuinely additional temporal question without
repeating the treatment-averaged increment figure. It can show a continued
redwood height advantage alongside slower later development. Do not imply
treatment-specific temporal evidence if the selected mean model constrains all
treatment changes to be equal: in that case collapse the bottom row to one
species-wise change panel, labeled as averaged across treatments. If temporal
evidence proves too fragile or secondary, retain the year-10 row as the main
figure and move the temporal display to the supplement.

Provisional caption structure: “Tallest-sprout development in sampled redwood and
tanoak clumps under four retained-overstory treatments. Upper panels show modeled
mean height at year 10; lower panels show later-minus-earlier annualized height
change. Points and ranges denote arithmetic means or contrasts and their 95%
confidence intervals [state site standardization/integration and uncertainty
method after selection]. Heights follow the tallest stem in each clump at each
visit, which need not be the same stem. Clumps are subsamples of 16 treatment
units in four sites; intervals describe mean uncertainty.” Define treatment
abbreviations in the final caption. Do not include significance arrows or infer
pairwise differences from overlapping mean intervals.

### 2. Optional companion: interval rates without averaging them away

If absolute growth rates matter for the management interpretation, use two
species panels with treatment on the x-axis and paired points for years 1–5
and 5–10, in m yr^-1^, with uncertainty. A light connector within each treatment
can show the interval change; it is not a continuous annual growth trajectory.
Use the same vertical scale for both species. Prefer equally weighted site
summaries as subdued observed context, with four site symbols per treatment,
over a dense cloud that makes hundreds of clumps look like treatment replicates.
Label observed summaries separately from model estimates and omit them if they
obscure the intervals.

This is an alternative temporal view or a supplement, not a second mandatory
main-text figure duplicating the lower row above. It preserves the thesis's
approximate 0.80-to-0.67 redwood and 0.39-to-0.34 tanoak story while allowing the
revised analysis to reveal treatment dependence. Keep full estimates, interval
definitions, planned contrasts, and sensitivity evidence in a companion table.
No invented confidence limits or schematic results are needed at this stage.

## Initial review conclusion

The thesis provides credible preliminary evidence that selected leading redwood
sprouts attained greater height under lighter retention and continued developing
under the higher-retention treatments. Its model/prose mismatch, selected-clump
sampling target, imposed temporal structure, and limited treatment replication
prevent us from carrying its precision and significance language forward unchanged.
The proposed tests separate changes to biological response assumptions from
changes to covariance and prediction targets. A compact size-plus-time display
can then complement RD02 without implying that tall sprouts alone establish
successful cohort recruitment or a long-term retention threshold. Model choice,
interval calibration, and final captions remain open until these tests are run.

## Phase One: audited inputs and human review {#rd03-phase-one}

Can we trace every modeled clump to the workbook, and what population can those
records describe? This first phase implements the audit and export prerequisites
in the selection sequence. Phase Two will fit the reference and limited
design/covariance candidates; later selection, bootstrap uncertainty, and display
acceptance follow that comparison. The phases make the existing sequence
explicit without accepting any candidate model in advance.

We exported both workbook sheets, the saved wide measurements with original and
renumbered identifiers, the historical response frames, and plain prediction
references in thesis R 4.3.2. The exporter checks every imported column against
the workbook and reproduces the saved long frames. It preserves the historical
factor levels (LIDE, SESE; GS, LD, HA, HD), row order, and missing values. No fitted
model crosses the publication boundary. The manifest protects the workbook,
saved objects, import/model sources, Methods, and existing thesis environment.
The thesis startup still reports its existing synchronization, locale, and
package-build warnings; no packages or lockfiles were changed. Replaying the
shared exporter also rewrote the existing fuel/regeneration RDS files with a
UTF-8 serialization header. Read-back comparisons with the committed baseline
confirmed identical R objects, and the historical CSV checksums are unchanged;
those analyses therefore require no numerical refresh.

The following audit runs in publication R 4.6.2 using only exported measurements.
An ordinary render reads saved audit tables; `-P recompute:true` refreshes these
deterministic calculations. Phase One has no fitting branch, so `refit:true` is
rejected to prevent it being mistaken for a completed model analysis.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-audit-setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dplyr); library(tidyr) })
if (isTRUE(params$refit)) stop("Phase One audits inputs only; no publication fitting is implemented yet.")
recompute <- isTRUE(params$recompute)
input <- "inputs/thesis/sprouts"
out <- "outputs/sprouts/phase-one"
read_audit <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(out, paste0(name, ".csv")), check.names = FALSE)
write_audit <- function(x, name) write.csv(x, file.path(out, paste0(name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
if (recompute) {
  dir.create(out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  d <- readRDS(file.path(input, "measurements.rds"))
  raw <- readRDS(file.path(input, "workbook-all.rds"))
  tallest <- readRDS(file.path(input, "workbook-tallest.rds"))
  frames <- readRDS(file.path(input, "historical-frames.rds"))
}
```

### Identity, repeated measurements, and interval definitions

We require unique original clump keys and a one-to-one map to the saved clump
IDs. Each macro plot must belong to one site and treatment, each site must have
all four treatments, and every clump must have three heights and two increments.
The numerical checks below use a tolerance of 10^-12^ m yr^-1^ for spreadsheet
roundoff; no height or increment is replaced or rounded in the input.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-identity-checks
if (recompute) {
  keys <- raw[c("Site", "Plot", "Species", "Tree")]
  macros <- distinct(d, plot, site, treat, original_plot)
  err5 <- max(abs(d$ht_inc5 - (d$ht5 - d$ht1) / 4))
  err10 <- max(abs(d$ht_inc10 - (d$ht10 - d$ht5) / 5))
  height_index <- match(paste(frames$dht$tree, frames$dht$year),
    paste(rep(d$tree, each = 3), rep(c(1, 5, 10), nrow(d))))
  inc_index <- match(paste(frames$dinc$tree, frames$dinc$year),
    paste(rep(d$tree, each = 2), rep(c(5, 10), nrow(d))))
  checks <- data.frame(check = c("Unique original site/plot/species/clump keys",
    "Unique saved clump IDs and source rows", "16 macros, one treatment per site",
    "Three historical heights per clump", "Two historical increments per clump",
    "Year-10 frame matches wide heights", "Years 1-5 increment = (H5-H1)/4",
    "Years 5-10 increment = (H10-H5)/5"),
    passed = c(!anyDuplicated(keys), !anyDuplicated(d$tree) && !anyDuplicated(d$source_row),
      nrow(macros) == 16L && !anyDuplicated(macros$plot) &&
        all(table(macros$site, macros$treat) == 1),
      nrow(frames$dht) == 3L * nrow(d) && !anyNA(height_index) &&
        !anyDuplicated(frames$dht[c("tree", "year")]) &&
        all(frames$dht$ht == c(t(as.matrix(d[c("ht1", "ht5", "ht10")])))[height_index]),
      nrow(frames$dinc) == 2L * nrow(d) && !anyNA(inc_index) &&
        !anyDuplicated(frames$dinc[c("tree", "year")]) &&
        all(frames$dinc$ht_inc == c(t(as.matrix(d[c("ht_inc5", "ht_inc10")])))[inc_index]),
      nrow(frames$dht10) == nrow(d) && !anyDuplicated(frames$dht10$tree) &&
        all(frames$dht10$ht == d$ht10[match(frames$dht10$tree, d$tree)]),
      err5 < 1e-12, err10 < 1e-12))
  stopifnot(all(checks$passed))
  write_audit(checks, "identity-checks")
}
knitr::kable(read_audit("identity-checks"))
```

All available workbook rows are accounted for in the saved analysis. The
`Age10all` sheet supplies 692 clumps, while `Age10tallest50tpha` contains a
320-row subset with the same original keys and heights. The latter has ten
clumps per site/treatment/species cell and ranks 1–10; it is an outcome-selected
subset, not additional replication or an attrition record. We retain the full
692-row cohort for the planned comparison and do not apply the workbook's
saved display filter. The original plot numbers and clump labels remain
available alongside the saved globally unique `plot` and `tree` factors.

We count clumps within the actual treatment units because these counts reveal
sampling composition without treating clumps as independent treatment replicates.
The selected-height subset is counted separately to expose the selection.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-cohort-counts
if (recompute) {
  counts <- d |> group_by(site, treat, spp) |>
    summarise(n_clumps = n(), n_missing_height = sum(is.na(ht1) | is.na(ht5) | is.na(ht10)),
      n_tallest_subset = sum(in_tallest_sheet), .groups = "drop")
  stopifnot(nrow(counts) == 32L, sum(counts$n_clumps) == 692L,
    all(counts$n_tallest_subset == 10L), sum(d$in_tallest_sheet) == nrow(tallest),
    all(tallest$HT10rank <= 10), all(d$in_tallest_sheet == (d$ht_rnk10 <= 10)))
  write_audit(counts, "cohort-counts")
}
knitr::kable(read_audit("cohort-counts"))
```

There are 334 redwood and 358 tanoak clumps, 2,076 height observations, and
1,384 increments across four sites and 16 macro plots. Redwood treatment totals
range from 72 to 91, and tanoak totals from 78 to 95. The Methods describes
approximately 25 clumps per species per macro plot, rather than an exact initial
roster. The available files cannot explain differences from that approximate
target. Complete rows do not establish complete follow-up of the original cohort.

### Response support and recoverable sampling information

We check missingness and support before considering response families. This also
makes the distinction between recorded interval change and growth of one
continuously tracked leader explicit: the measurements follow the tallest sprout
in each clump at each visit.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-response-support
if (recompute) {
  support <- bind_rows(lapply(c("ht1", "ht5", "ht10", "ht_inc5", "ht_inc10"), function(v) {
    x <- d[[v]]
    data.frame(variable = v, n = length(x), missing = sum(is.na(x)),
      zero = sum(x == 0, na.rm = TRUE), negative = sum(x < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      minimum = min(x, na.rm = TRUE), maximum = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      unit = if (startsWith(v, "ht_inc")) "m yr-1" else "m")
  }))
  stopifnot(all(support$missing == 0), all(is.finite(support$minimum)),
    all(support$minimum > 0))
  write_audit(support, "response-support")
}
knitr::kable(read_audit("response-support"), digits = 4)
```

All recorded heights and increments are positive. This removes a support-based
objection to a positive increment family on these rows, but does not establish
that Gamma is appropriate. The planned Gaussian increment reference remains
unchanged. Neither valid negative increments in a future corrected input nor
missing/dead clumps should be silently removed or recoded to fit a family.

The workbook's `ResidRWonClumpYN` was omitted from the thesis import. We recover
its numeric codes as `residual_rw`, retaining NA for tanoak. A code of 1 denotes
residual redwood on the clump according to the column label; its timing and field
protocol still need confirmation. We tabulate both codes and missing values
before proposing any adjustment.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-sampling-composition
if (recompute) {
  composition <- d |> group_by(spp, treat) |>
    summarise(n_clumps = n(), code_0 = sum(residual_rw == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      code_1 = sum(residual_rw == 1, na.rm = TRUE), missing = sum(is.na(residual_rw)),
      .groups = "drop")
  stopifnot(all(is.na(d$residual_rw[d$spp == "LIDE"])),
    all(d$residual_rw[d$spp == "SESE"] %in% c(0, 1)))
  write_audit(composition, "sampling-composition")
}
knitr::kable(read_audit("sampling-composition"))
```

Redwood has 197 code-0 and 137 code-1 clumps; tanoak has 358 missing indicators,
so its missing values must not be treated as code 0. All 91 GS redwood clumps
have code 0. LD has 41/31, HA 35/52, and HD 30/54 code-0/code-1 clumps. Thus the
redwood indicator is treatment-associated and lacks overlap in GS. Adjusting for
it would change the treatment question and cannot identify every
within-stratum treatment comparison. We have no area-wide stratum frequencies
or inclusion probabilities from which to calculate sampling weights.

### Descriptive context and historical reference

We summarize each species within each macro plot first, then weight the four
sites equally for a descriptive treatment summary. These are observed sample
means, not fitted estimates or confidence intervals. Duration weighting uses
four and five years, so the years 1–10 annual rate equals `(H10-H1)/9`.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-observed-context
if (recompute) {
  observed <- d |> group_by(site, plot, treat, spp) |>
    summarise(n_clumps = n(), height1 = mean(ht1), height5 = mean(ht5), height10 = mean(ht10),
      increment_1_5 = mean(ht_inc5), increment_5_10 = mean(ht_inc10),
      period_change = mean(ht_inc10 - ht_inc5),
      annual_rate_1_10 = mean((4 * ht_inc5 + 5 * ht_inc10) / 9), .groups = "drop")
  stopifnot(nrow(observed) == 32L,
    max(abs(observed$annual_rate_1_10 - (observed$height10 - observed$height1) / 9)) < 1e-12)
  write_audit(observed, "observed-site-means")
}
knitr::kable(read_audit("observed-site-means"), digits = 3)
```

The equal-site summary helps assess the direction of change without allowing
larger sampled cohorts to dominate a treatment. The four site means in the
preceding table retain the variation behind each treatment summary.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-observed-treatment-context
if (recompute) {
  treatment <- observed |> group_by(spp, treat) |>
    summarise(n_sites = n(), across(c(height10, increment_1_5, increment_5_10,
      period_change, annual_rate_1_10), mean), .groups = "drop")
  stopifnot(all(treatment$n_sites == 4L))
  write_audit(treatment, "observed-treatment-means")
}
knitr::kable(read_audit("observed-treatment-means"), digits = 3)
```

The observed year-10 means decrease from GS through LD and HA to HD in both
species: redwood spans 10.480 to 5.929 m, and tanoak 5.213 to 3.142 m. The later
interval has a lower observed annual increment in all eight cells. Redwood
changes range from -0.159 to -0.066 m yr^-1^, compared with -0.048 to -0.037 for
tanoak. These summaries motivate testing treatment-specific temporal means;
they do not establish significant contrasts or validate a particular covariance
structure.

For traceability, the historical table below contains direct saved-model
predictions checked against the fixed-effect design matrix in thesis R. Its SEs
are historical model-based mean SEs; they do not validate four-site coverage or
establish any new contrast. Period codes 5 and 10 mean years 1–5 and 5–10.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-historical-reference
knitr::kable(read.csv(file.path(input, "historical-predictions.csv")) |>
  select(model_id, treat, spp, period, estimate, se, unit), digits = 4)
```

### Human review and Phase Two handoff {#rd03-handoff}

The available records now support a reproducible analysis of the **selected,
recorded clump cohort**, retaining all 692 rows. They do not resolve whether the
workbook was assembled only from surviving or otherwise eligible clumps. We
found no original enrollment roster, mortality/absence ledger, per-visit leader
IDs, or inclusion probabilities in the workbook, import/model sources, Methods,
work log, or relevant repository notes; the workbook has no cell comments or
additional sheets documenting those events. The tally of roughly 25 clumps per
species per macro plot is insufficient to reconstruct an attrition denominator.
These are missing field-history evidence, not failed numerical checks.

Human review should confirm the residual-tree code definition and timing, explain
unequal clump counts if original records exist, and decide whether the recorded
cohort is the intended target for exploratory fitting. No sampling weights,
zero-height replacements, survival claims, or unobserved leader histories have
been inferred. If new field information changes inclusion or measurements,
refresh the export and this audit before fitting.

The next agent should read this section and the [candidate plan](#rd03-model-plan),
verify export integrity with
`python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --inputs-only --protected`, and use
`inputs/thesis/sprouts/measurements.rds` in the publication environment. Preserve
the exported factor coding and original ID crosswalk; use all rows, not the
tallest-ten subset. The historical frames and 24 prediction cells provide
reproduction references, not publication estimates. Start Phase Two with the
thesis reference fits and the limited site-blocking, species-macro covariance,
and increment temporal-mean alternatives on identical rows. Use ML for
fixed-effect comparisons, retain design clustering, and record convergence,
Hessian, variance boundaries, second-optimizer agreement, and leave-one-site-out
sensitivity. Do not add an unidentified full two-period covariance on top of
unrestricted residual variances and a clump intercept.

Before reporting publication means, resolve observed-site versus exchangeable-site
standardization and predeclare contrast families and multiplicity handling.
Keep residual-tree adjustment as an explicitly conditional sensitivity, subject
to code validation and the GS overlap limitation. Bootstrap calibration and
final displays follow model review; RT02, M02, and D02 remain queued. Human
review should precede the next phase.

Phase One establishes traceable inputs and exposes a consequential selection
limitation that complete analytical frames alone concealed. It also recovers a
sampling indicator that can inform a carefully bounded sensitivity. The main
scientific limitation remains generalization beyond the selected recorded clumps;
model fitting cannot recover the missing field history or establish survival.
